utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. First thing I'd like to do, should not take too much time, is to deal with the exhibits that were produced through the last witness, that would be D70 -- 27 up to and including D30.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked Madam Registrar to -- to send the list. These are just the exhibits I would like to deal with at this moment, only these last four. Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I was just handed the list as I walked in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I have until next session to have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear from you then at -- just after the next break. I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just wish to raise the issue of the provision of the consolidated witness statement of the witness, which was completed last night. We sent a copy to the Defence last night when it was completed, the signed -- I have the signed version. It's been e-mailed to the Defence, and I apologise, I thought it had been e-mailed earlier, but it wasn't. I've also asked whether the Defence object to the Trial Chamber being provided with copies. I have copies here for everyone in the court. If the Defence want their signed hard copy, they can get it right away, and if they consent it to going to the Trial Chamber, we can also provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber will see whether there's consent and then they'll receive it. We'll then now have a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. The protective measures sought for the next witness to be called by the Prosecution are granted. The reasons, to be given orally, will come at a later stage. The -- Mr. Re, the pseudonym would be 23 or would it be another number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, 23 is the number -- so witness 60. Then we'll -- yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I mention one matter very briefly in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind the parties to switch off their microphones when the witness is answering any questions. Good afternoon, Witness, Witness 60, because that's how I'm going to call you. Since the Chamber has decided that you'll testify under a pseudonym and with face and voice distortion, that does mean that no one sees your face outside of this courtroom, no one can hear your own voice, and that we'll address you as "Witness 60." Witness 60, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher now hands out the text of this solemn declaration to you. Make I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Witness 60. You'll first be examined by - you, Mr. Re - by Mr. Re, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness 60. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Yes, I can hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: First thing I want to show you is a -- what's called a pseudonym sheet which has your name and details on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we go into -- do we have to go into closed session to display that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, usually the pseudonym sheet is shown to the witness, and then the usual question is whether what is written on this piece of paper, whether that is the name and the date of birth of the witness; and he's then invited to either confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether we need to go into closed session because of the display on the screen? No. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there will be no display, it will just be shown to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Look on the screen. The Exhibit will be called 1216 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P37, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and under seal. Does it already appear in front of you? Let me ... one second, there it comes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you now see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are those details correct? Is that you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, but the year of birth is not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 60, where were you and your family living in January, February, March, April 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We were living in the village of Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many Serbian families or households were in Dasinovac as of the beginning of April -- beginning of 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: About ten -- or rather, seven or eight Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many Albanian households or families were in that same area as of January 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: There were many of them, possibly between 200 and 300 Albanian households.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of property did your family own in Dasinovac in 1998? Was it a house? A farm? Or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We had around eight hectares of arable land. We had outbuildings, we had a house, stables. We kept cattle, pigs, bees. We grew wheat, potatoes, and things like that. We had a regular farming life in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Approximately how many animals did you own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We had 30, 40 sheep; one cow; one horse; 30 chickens; five pigs; we had about 20 beehives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have an orchard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We had a large orchard with lots of plum trees, apple trees, walnuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about agricultural machinery, did you have any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We had some old machines, but we didn't use them much. We did the land manually more or less, and we use our horse for that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long has the property been in your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: As far as I know, sometime after the Second World War my grandfather moved to that land. I apologise, after the First World War or probably 1914, 1918.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about things that were happening in Dasinovac and the area in late 1997 and early 1998. You were -- were you aware of an organisation called the Kosovo Liberation Army, the UCK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes. We heard about it, and we knew that they were in the area where we were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you hear about it, and when did you first hear about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We heard first -- for the first time about them sometime between 1997/1998 when they used to stop people. There was lots of talk about that. They also started attacking the police station in Rznic, which is not very far from my home, and, therefore, we knew that the KLA was operating in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise, but can I remind Mr. Re if he's eliciting evidence of this kind to identify the source of the information, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was actually my next follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to be a little more specific about the sources of your information. You said you heard about them, and they started to -- when they used to stop people. What was it you heard and who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: In the spring of 1978 or 1979, they stopped Dragoslav Stojanovic, they searched him, mistreated him, and then released him. I heard it from him personally, and that is how I knew he had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we check the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said -- or the translation says "1978 or 1979." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, 1977. I'm sorry, between 1977 and 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mean 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten years instead of 30 years ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was about ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from stopping Dragoslav Stojanovic, did you hear of the KLA stopping other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see, yourself, the KLA stopping anybody before April 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you know about the KLA attacking the Rznic police station, like when was it? Did you see it yourself or did you hear about it; if so, who did you hear it from and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I heard it in the spring of 1998, people were talking about it, and it was on television and in the press as well. It was on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your knowledge, January, February, March 1998, about the presence or otherwise of the KLA in the area around Dasinovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, people were saying that they were over in Glodjane and that their HQ was there, too. In addition to those attacks on the police, they also -- one stopped Dragoslav, as I have mentioned, but I didn't personally encounter them or see them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were people saying about them being over there in Gllogjan and the headquarters being there? Try and be as - I know it's been a long time - but as precise as you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, in March, people from my village and the surrounding villages started leaving the area for fear of the KLA. People were scared. There were cars driving through the villages at night, and the police had stopped coming to our villages by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you know they were leaving for fear of the KLA? What's your information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: There was fear. They were even trying to talk us into leaving, but my father was ill at the time; on the 8th of April, he eventually died. And that's why we refused to leave. We were too busy dealing with my father's illness. We ignored all of the stories that were circulating. We got on well with our own neighbours in our own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said there was fear. I want you to describe to the Trial Chamber -- tell the Trial Chamber what the fear was. What was the -- what was the source of the fear? Why were people experiencing fear and what was giving them fear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: They were scared by the presence of the KLA in the area. There had been frequent attacks on the police station. People felt fear. I'm not sure how to explain. We were scared, too, despite which we stayed on in the village for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they scared of?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is about the third time that Mr. Re has asked for opinion evidence from this witness without laying a foundation for it. I've tried to hesitate but it's not, with respect, appropriate without laying a foundation as to what the source of the information was to be seeking to elicit opinion evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, it's true what Mr. Emmerson says. And I left it for a moment in order to find out whether your next question would resolve the matter, but it did not yet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which people are you talking about, the ones you say experienced fear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: At the time, there had been an attack on the houses in the village of Ratis and the people were saying that the KLA from Glodjane had done that. A grenade was thrown in Malesa Culafic's [Realtime transcript read in error "Malis Suvakic's"] house was targeted. This house is near the elementary school near the centre of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whose houses were attacked? How do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if you know first, try to find out the source of knowledge, then at least we know what we are talking about. How did you learn about this attack on Malesa Culafic's house?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wonder if we might concentrate on the name because that's not the name as it appears on the transcript that I heard through the headphones, and it is a name that we're already familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will clarify, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you clarify that and seek an answer to that question; also to the question where he said, they tried to talk us out or -- or I don't know what was the exact wording -- they were even trying to talk us into leaving. We do not know who tried to do so. If you would resolve the matter, as well, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness D [sic], whose house was attacked in Ratis? Just the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Malesa Culafic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you find out about that? Who told you or did you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: First the neighbours came to our place and told us about it, and then afterwards I went there myself. I went to that house, but that family left the village soon after.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they a Serb family? An Albanian family? Or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: They were a Serb family.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you told who had attacked the house with a grenade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: The only thing that was said was that someone had attacked the house. There was nothing more specific. Newspapers said there had been a terror attack against that house, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said a grenade was thrown at the house. Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I heard that from Malesa Culafic's wife. She said that, first a grenade had been thrown behind the house, and then a mortar was used to target the house. It was by pure coincidence, she claimed, that she had survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Page 31 of the transcript, today you said: "Well, in March people from my village and the surrounding villages started leaving the area for fear of the KLA. People were scared." I just want to take you back to that. Which people left the villages and how do you know that they left the villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Serbs were leaving the village. I know that those were Serbs because the first family to leave was from Ratis, the Culafic family; the next to leave were the Stijovics; and they were followed by all the other Serbs in the village. They left that village and all the surrounding villages, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And at page 31, a bit further down, you said: "There was fear. They were even trying to talk us into leaving." My question was: "How did you know they were leaving for fear of the KLA?" And you said: "There was fear. They were even trying to talk us into leaving but my father was ill at the time." Now, who was trying to talk you into leaving and what did the people who were trying to talk you into leaving do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: They were trying to convince us -- the Serbs were, to leave. They were scared. They were saying that it wasn't safe to stay. After the attack on the Culafic house, there was an attack of Slobo Prascevic, a former police officer, and Dimitrije Radovic. He left afterwards. So did Pavle Djukic. Those people were trying to convince us that it was no longer safe to stay. They were saying, Look, all sorts of things are happening here. It's a much better idea for you to leave and find a safer, more peaceful place for you to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify. Who was trying to convince you to leave? Who was telling you it was safer to go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Our neighbours, the Serbs from our village and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just mentioned an attack on the Culafic house. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you know about that and how you know about it -- or put it the other way around: How you know about it and what you know? Were you told? Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, isn't it true the witness just told us that he went first to the neighbours that he heard then; and that he then went to the place himself and he told us about the grenade. I mean, there was quite a lot of evidence which gives a rather clear source.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. Is that the -- if that's the -- the name was different on the transcript. If that's the same one, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is the same that's why I clarified the error on the transcript, and the witness corrected it and gave us the name which we're familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one you mentioned was an attack on Slobo Prascevic. Same question: What do you know about that? Who told you? Did you see it? Were you there? When was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I didn't see it. All I know is the story told me by Pavle Djukic. He said this had occurred quite near his house. He said he had seen five or six armed people dressed in black. He claimed to have recognised among those people Xhevdet Sadikaj. So there's little that I actually know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What -- were you told when this had occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry, but there's a stipulation in relation to when this occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, yes, there were two days, one day difference, and then the parties agreed on what day the event which, from what I remember, was an attack on the car took place. I think even by heart, I think it was the 22nd or the 23rd of April if I'm not -- or March or something --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 2nd March it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2nd, okay. Then I'm -- I'll -- please proceed. I'll give you the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you living in Dasinovac with your mother, father, brother, and sister-in-law in January, February, March, up to the 8th of April -- up to the 10th of April when your father died in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did your sister-in-law leave the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Sometime around the 17th or the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did she leave the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: She had some health problems, so my younger brother and I had to take her to see a doctor in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did something happen on your way to Pec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, at Ljubarda, as we were passing through -- driving through on our way to Pec, on our left there were about ten people standing in a meadow. One of them produced a pistol, pulled out a gun, and fired a shot in our direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember what these people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I can't say. Maybe I was too scared to notice, but all I remember is all of them wearing black or that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they men, or women, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: A group of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them or know any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you continue to live in Dasinovac after your -- after you took your sister-in-law to Pec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, we continued to live there until the 22nd or 23rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened a few days before the 22nd or 23rd of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I started worrying about our safety. There were none of our Serb neighbours left in the area, so I went to the village to seek information -- I mean, Dasinovac itself, but no one was willing to come out and talk to me, none of the people there. I only came across women and children. That same day, however, Isuf Sadikaj, a neighbour of mine, came looking for me. He said, I know you've been to see me, I know you've been looking for me, and there's nothing I can tell you. Just stay in your home. Don't take the road to Decani because those people from Glodjane are in control of that road. I then proceeded to ask him who exactly was in control of what and who those people were. He said, Just stay at home and don't worry. We'll look after you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you understand him to mean by the expression, "Those people from Gllogjan"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I asked him a number of questions: Who are they? What are they? And he said, Ask no questions. Just stay at home, don't go anywhere, don't leave home, and certainly make sure not to take that road to Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, what did you understand to mean -- what was your understanding of those people from Gllogjan? Apart from what he said to you, what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, I simply thought that the safest thing to do was to just follow his instructions. He said he was speaking on behalf of the village. I took him seriously. We headed back home and never again tried to leave home or our property.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that a few days before the 22nd or 23rd of April, you "started worrying about our safety." Why did you start worrying about your safety? What were your fears?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: My house is on an elevation. Not far from my property, there is a road leading from Dasinovac to the village of Bardonici. We used to see armed men walking along that road, and at night there would be cars speeding by at break-neck speed, but we never tried to approach any of them or make contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe these armed men you saw walking along the road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, those were - how can I say this? -- it was quite far from my house but there were groups of men passing by, sometimes two, sometimes three, and one could see them -- one could see their rifles slung over their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: It seemed to me that they were wearing black all the time, but I was too far to notice any details in terms of their clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was this a usual or an unusual thing, that there were armed men with rifles slung over their shoulders walking past your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: It was unusual, the reason being there were not many hunters in that village. Most of those were Serbs, although there were both Serb and Albanian hunters, but these were men I'd never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did this cause you fear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, our fear was caused by everything that was going on around us; the attack on Prascevic and then that house in Ratis, which is not too far from my own house. Those men passing by, and then the words told me by that neighbour, which caused me a great amount of fear, to me and to all of us, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to clarify which words are you speaking -- are you referring to when you say "the words told to me by the neighbour"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Sadikaj Isuf, his words. He said, Don't leave home. Stay at home. We'll look after you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know or recognise any of the men walking past your home armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know where they were coming from or going to or why they were walking along that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. They seemed to be patrolling the area between the cemetery and as far as I could see in the direction of Bardonici. They would walk as far as the cemetery and walk back the same way, and this was quite a frequent occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But what happened on the 22nd of April, 1998? Were you at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your neighbours doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you had in mind. I'm slightly confused there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anyone called Nrec Hajdare or Gjon Fazli Hajdare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, those are my next-door neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see them doing anything; if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, that day at about 4.00 -- perhaps it was past 4.00, I saw Nrec Hajdare, he came out of the cellar, and Gjon Hajdare was with him, they brought up a huge machine-gun, and there was a third man with them wearing black and a black cap. He seemed to be in a hurry while Gjon was trying to get him to slow down. He was pulling him back, sort of trying to get him not to hurry. A little while later, there was a fourth voice that was heard, it was a hoarse voice saying, Listen, don't go anywhere without my orders. And then the next thing he said was, Listen, we're setting out. We'll catch all of them and kill them. Let's get on with it. A little while later, there was this muted shot from some sort of a shot-gun or a rifle, a muted sound of a shot muffled. I was scared, and I was concerned about my family and my neighbour. I got all of them to go to a nearby forest to take cover. There was a great amount of fear in the air the moment the shot was heard, and many people headed towards our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just take you back for a moment. You said, "We'll catch all of them and kill them." Who did you understand them to be referring to when they said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: At the time, my family and my neighbour were the only Serbs around, so the reference was probably to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who were the many people who headed towards your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Albanians. There were some of our neighbours there, but I did not see any of our neighbours carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were any people in that group carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, there were people carrying weapons, long-barrel weapons. There were some long barrels there in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Some had a mixture of camouflage uniform and civilian clothes; the top being camouflage and the bottoms civilian. Some were wearing black. As my fear at the time was great, there seemed to be very many of them. We were really scared, and we ran to the woods to seek cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "we," are you referring to your family members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, my family members and my neighbour who was there with his wife and his one-year-old child. They were visiting us at the time when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know or recognise any of the armed people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How close did they get to your family before you decided to go -- to run to the woods to seek cover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, believe me, we were really scared, and this is not the sort of thing that I was focusing on. But as soon as we heard the shot, we ran to the woods, too, to seek cover there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you give an approximate figure of how many people were in that group and how many appeared to you to be armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: It was quite a large group. It's difficult for me to say how large specifically. My fear was too great. I couldn't think in those terms, I couldn't even look back to see what was going on in our house. We simply reached this grove near our home, and we spent that entire night there. Around this wood, one could hear Albanian voices talking and laughing. We could hear someone drive up to our house in a car and turning around there, that sort of thing, and noises.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you speak Albanian and read and write Albanian then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I spoke Albanian, was quite fluent, and I was able to both read and write Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you, your family, and your neighbours sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We spent the entire night in the woods. It was bitterly cold, and the small baby was crying. The baby's father even tried to smother the baby at one point, but we managed to get him not to do that. We tried to head through the woods towards Ratis, but at the far end of the wood we noticed some people standing there smoking. There were three or four of them, which made us change our minds and walk back to where we had come from. We spent the entire night in the woods, and at about daybreak we decided to head back home and see what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened when you got home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Once we had reached our house, we realised that no one had entered the house the previous night. We stayed there. My mother brewed us some coffee, but we ran out of firewood at one point. My mother said, Off I go to get some firewood. And I said, Please, mother, don't go. It was daybreak, it was light, and I said, Don't go, someone will see you. And she said, Don't worry about me, nothing will happen to me. As soon as she was out of that door, we heard someone say in Serbian, Good morning. And then three of our neighbours came in following her.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Azir Sadikaj was the first to get in, then Gjon Hajdare, and then Fazlija and Qaus -- no, I'm sorry, not Qaus, Qamil Romaj [phoen]. They were in civilian clothes. They were concerned and they were friendly towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, none of them had any weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did they come to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: As soon as they came, they said, Listen, neighbours, the situation is very bad. These men from Glodjane have come and took over the village, or are, rather, in the village. We somehow managed to persuade them last night and gave them guarantees for your safety. The situation is very bad, and it seems that you will have to leave the village immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons in your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you about your weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, they told us that they had persuaded the men from Glodjane, and I must emphasise that they always used this phrase, "Those from Glodjane or the army from Glodjane." So in return for our release, they demanded that we surrender our weapons in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just specify by who -- who is the "they" you're referring to? In return for our release, they demanded that we surrender. Are you referring to the three neighbours or to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: According to my neighbours, those from Glodjane had demanded that we turn in our weapons in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your response to what they said to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, at first we were worried. We asked them what had happened. Why was such a huge group of people rushing towards us the previous night? They said that was just for a moment. We could quickly manage to calm them down. And now they allow us to come to you and provide and offer guarantee for your safe leave out of the village, provided you hand in your weapons. After that, these three men left, and about a half an hour later my younger brother and I buried an old pistol and an old gun in the garden. When the three returned, they said, Hurry-up, we don't have much time. Don't you take any valuables with you like gold, money, and things like that. Nothing must be in the boot of your car, apart from the two rifles that you have to surrender in the centre of the village for those men to see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We listened to them. We didn't take any of our belongings with us, apart from our identification cards - and I mean my brother and I. We put the two rifles into the boot of the car, and neither I nor my brother had noticed that the neighbour who was with us put in a little bag with baby's stuff like nappies and things like that. We were followed all the way to the village. One of the neighbours, one in front of us and the other one was behind of us, while my family and the third neighbour were in the car. The first man was carrying something yellow in his hand looking like a towel, and he was waving it as a kind of sign or recognition or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When your family left your house that day, what did you leave behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We left everything behind, everything we had, the cattle, the wealth that we had, everything remained there. I must say nothing apart from our identity cards did my brother and I take from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you go with those three neighbours in your brother's car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We went to Decani from Rausic and reported at the Decani police station everything that had happened to us. Then from Decani, we went to Pec. At my sister's place and with some friends, we stayed for two or three days. Then we went back to Decani and tried to find accommodation in the vicinity of the Decani monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you find accommodation there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We found an accommodation, an old holiday resort near Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe the accommodation, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: It was a holiday resort of a company from Djakovica. These were prefabricated bungalows made of wood. There were other Serbian families there. I even remember that there was a Muslim family. They later left, but I don't know where they went. All the peoples staying in those bungalows were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why were those Serb families staying there? What did they tell you about the reasons why they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: All of them had to leave their villages as a result of terrorist activities in our municipality at the time. Some of them came before us, some came after us, but all of them were from the villages in the area where I came from. There were people from Papracani, Ratis, Gornji Ratis, Dasinovac, Ljubarda.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Don't tell me where you went, but just tell me how long you and your family stayed in that refugee accommodation for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We stayed until 1999 in Decani, but I must tell you that at times only we lived there. We spent most of our time at my sister's in Pec. I also went to Podgorica; I worked on the coastline. I spent a lot of time in the monastery as well because I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you leave that accommodation finally, as best as you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Sometime in the -- in mid-June 1999, at the very end of the bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you next go back to your land in Dasinovac, after leaving in the manner you've just described on -- about the 23rd of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I went back for the first time in September or more probably October of that same year. I went back simply after asking some policemen, Is it safe to go to Dasinovac? And they said, Why wouldn't it be? You can go freely there. So my younger brother and I, a neighbour of ours, and a woman first went to our house, then we went to their houses. We spent altogether about ten minutes in each of the houses, and then we went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you not go back until either September or October 1998? Was there anything stopping you going back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that at the time there was fierce fighting at the time. I don't know how to describe it because on many occasions whenever I wanted to go to my place, residential place, from Pec, there were roadblocks. It sometimes took two or three days to reach Decani from Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whose roadblocks were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: The KLA. There were official reports that the KLA had attacked the police and the army. There was shooting. People were saying that it wasn't safe. Even the police didn't allow us to travel between Pec and Decani because it was not safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see these roadblocks, KLA roadblocks, yourself, or was it something you heard about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. I never saw those roadblocks because I simply didn't want to take any chances. If somebody tells me, Don't go there, it's dangerous, then I obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it the Serb police who were saying, Don't take that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you described a moment ago there being fierce fighting. Who was the fighting between?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Between the Albanian terrorists and most probably police. Believe me, I never wanted to become involved in things like that. I'm not that kind of person. I was living very nicely and peacefully in Pec during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, describe the state of your property when you went back with your younger brother in about September or October 1998. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: The property was completely destroyed. There were about 2 hectares under wheat. It had been harvestless [as interpreted]. The stables were completely destroyed. I mean for sheep, for cows, for horses. Some outbuildings also were destroyed. The house was totally demolished. There was -- there were no doors or windows. We didn't find any of our belongings in the house. The tools that we had were disappeared -- had disappeared. The well, water-well, was destroyed. The forest had been felled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about your animals, were they there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, we didn't find any of the cattle that we used to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the other animals? You described a horse, a cow, five pigs, some chickens.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. There was nothing. We didn't find anything. The place where beehives were was empty, the stables were destroyed, so there was nothing left of the livestock that we had. We didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said your house was totally demolished. Can you give a better description of what you saw when you went back there. What do you mean by "demolished"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: The house was totally empty. There was just a pile of rubbish in one of the rooms. There were no windows or doors. They even ripped out the electrical wiring from the walls. There were no sockets, there were no bulbs, nothing. The house had graffiti on it, UCK or KLA and other things were written on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it have a roof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: The roof was destroyed, but the house had not been set on fire. Part of the roof was missing and part of the roof was there, as if someone had been taking tiles one by one and removing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about personal effects such as clothing, photographs, things like that, were any of those remaining?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: We left everything, our documents, my father's photographs, our clothing, and we found nothing when we came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you ever recovered any of the things that you left behind on about the 23rd of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the next time you went -- when was the next time you were able to go to the property? You described going there in September or October 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: The next time I went was in 2001, and I went there escorted by Italian soldiers from KFOR. Then we went again in 2003; again we were escorted by both KFOR and the Albanian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does your family still own the property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, we still own the property.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On that day you went back and stayed there for about ten minutes, you said you went to two other properties and stayed about ten minutes each there. Whose houses were those, and what did you see when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: First we went to the house of Radun Dabetic. His house was also destroyed, but there was some clothes and some old things in the house. And Novak Stijovic's house was completely empty and everything was destroyed, just as it was the case with my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a neighbour called Adzija Redzaj, forgive my pronunciation, and speaking to him sometime in 1998 after you had left your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: In 1998, after we had left the village, maybe two or three months later we accidentally met near Pec. We greeted each other. We were on good terms. I asked him to join me for a drink. I said, Come, neighbour, there's a Serbian cafe nearby. So without thinking for a second, he joined me. We sat down and I asked him how he was, how his family was, and he said, Don't ask me anything. I asked him, How is the situation in the village? And he said, I don't know. I had to leave the village just like you had. And I asked him, Why, what happened with our livestock and our property? And he told me, Neighbour, believe me, I don't know. Immediately after your departure from the village, a bit -- maybe half an hour later, Ramush Haradinaj came to the village and started shouting at Isuf and the rest of us in the village, Why did you let them go? Why did they leave? And then I asked him why you had to leave the village? And he said, Don't ask me anything. I had to leave all my property and leave the village. I had all my belongings in one plastic bag. And I asked him why was he shouting? He said, Don't ask me. We had problems because we let you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to separate two of the things you've said there. You said Ramush Haradinaj started shouting at Isuf. Is that Isuf Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the rest of us in the village, why did you let them go? Why did they leave? Stop you there. Did Adzija Redzaj tell you who Ramush Haradinaj was referring to when he said, "Why did you let them leave?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He only said that he was shouting at Isuf and the rest of them, but he didn't say specifically who he was shouting at and what happened next. He said only that when he came, he was very angry and said that no one else must leave, either our village or the neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And a moment ago, you said he said, Don't ask me anything. I had to leave all my property and leave the village. Were you referring to your friend Adzija Redzaj, as saying, he said, Don't ask me anything; that is, he told you, Don't ask me anything, he had to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Adzija told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, did you know Ramush Haradinaj at any point in your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I finished elementary school the first four years in Rznic, and his father had a shop some 200 metres from the school. I often went there. His father's name was Hilmi, if I remember correctly. He was a fine old gentleman, and we often went to his store almost every day. So it is possible and I think that Ramush Haradinaj used to come as well. I was very young at the time. And I didn't pay much attention to that. So I know him from the time when I was attending school in Rznic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the last time you think you saw him in person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I can't remember. I may have been 14 or 15 at the time, seventh or eighth grade perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about someone called - excuse me for one moment - someone called Milos Radunovic. Did you know someone called Milos Radunovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's a neighbour who lived in Dasinovac, a kilometre from my house perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Milos Radunovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: The day before I left my property and my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: He came sometime after 3.00 to see me, to my home, my family, visiting. Sometime past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how long did he stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Between 30 and 45 minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What means of transportation did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: He rode a bike.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And after 30 to 45 minutes, where did he go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: He said he would be on his way to see Slobodan Radosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you hear about what happened to Milos Radunovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, let's turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. How much time do you think you would still need, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Probably about 15 minutes, that's allowing for marking of two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you try to do it in approximately ten minutes and then we will have the break and then we, after the break, the Defence will have an opportunity to cross-examine the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you hear about what happened to Milos Radunovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: On the way from Dasinovaci to Decani, the day after -- the day I left my house, Xhevdet Sadikaj and I went as far as Rausic together and Xhevdet himself told me this, Yesterday those people from Glodjane caught Miroslav Radunovic as he was passing my house on a bike. They pulled him off the bike and said, Where have you been? We've been looking for you. Xhevdet claimed that he and his father had tried to help Milos, but they shoved them aside and told them not to get involved, that they had no business being there or doing anything. They drove back to Milos's house. They opened the boot of that car, and they told Milos, Okay, so what can you tell us now? These are weapons that we found at Milos Radunovic's house and then Xhevdet claims they said, Now we're off to get Slobo to catch Slobo and they were off to Slobo Radosevic's house. Soon after Xhevdet claims that a lot of shooting could be heard. I heard the same sounds of shooting but Xhevdet claims that 10 or 15 minutes after, he was at the juncture between Slobo and Xhevdet's house and the road to Decani -- actually, the road to Decani and the road to Glodjane and then he says he saw Slobo and Milos who had been captured already. Milos had been wounded in his arm and they were being taken to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the last time -- I withdraw that? Did you know Slobodan Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Perhaps seven or eight days before I left my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said you -- you heard the -- you said something about hearing the sounds of shooting. Can you just elaborate on that? What did you hear? What were you and where was the shooting coming from and about what time was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: It was the day before we left our house. Milos had gone on before us, 10 or 15 minutes previously; and after his departure there was a great deal of shooting from Slobo Radosevic's house, from those whereabouts. It went on for about 10 or 15 minutes. We didn't know at the time what exactly was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What else did Xhevdet Sadikaj tell you about his own situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Xhevdet said, I'm also involved in this army, but I disagree with these decisions. I'm not in favour of dealing with it like this. I'm in favour of a peaceful solution here. We're helping you to get out. He also said that he had seen Milka and Mika the day before and that they were fine, and that as soon as he took us to Rausic he would be back to help get the two of them out of the village as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come to that in a moment. Which army was he -- did you understand him to be referring to when he said, I'm also involved in this army but I disagree with these decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: He didn't tell me himself, but it was my understanding that he was a member of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What gave you that understanding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, that was the only army around at the time, paramilitary I mean, in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But did he tell you -- did he say anything to you about Isuf Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: He said, I am standing in for him and all will be fine that I had agreed with Isuf, whereas there had been no agreement between myself and Isuf Sadikaj, apart from his promise that we would not come to any harm, that we should just stay at home and that the village would look after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he tell you or did you have any understanding of what Xhevdet Sadikaj's position was within that army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. He didn't say, nor was able to infer anything about that. The only thing he did say was that he was at this time standing in for Isuf Sadikaj. Isuf Sadikaj is a very pleasant young man, same generation as me. We used to socialize. There is not a single bad thing I could possibly say about him, at the time or now for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you understand Isuf Sadikaj's position to be within that army and what did you understand to mean by, I am standing in for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Well, he said he was standing in for Isuf Sadikaj. That was all he said, and believe me, I'm not sure how to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you referred to - excuse me for one moment - Milka and Mika. Who were they? Not -- just their names, please, nothing else, what the names are, Milka and Mika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Do you want to know about their surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Milka Markovic and Mika Radunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the last time that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I can't remember about Mika. I saw Milka up to ten days before I left my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did Xhevdet Sadikaj tell you about the two of them when he had last seen them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: He assured me that day that he had seen them. He said, I saw them yesterday. They are fine. I'll try to get them out of the village, too. As soon as I leave you there, I'll go back and get them. Don't you worry about those two. I'm sure I'll manage. And I said, What about the rest of them? He said, I can't say. The two of them probably as soon as I am done leaving you there, I'll go back and get them, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to go into closed session for one -- in a moment. I'm just telegraphing where I'm going to get the witness to mark something on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before we do that, I just want you to clarify something. You said there were seven or eight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps already inform Madam Registrar which ones of these, so that loading takes less time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll do that. Onto -- P10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said there were seven or eight, ten or so Serb families in your village area. Just briefly tell -- I won't ask for the names at the moment, but tell the Trial Chamber (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: (redacted) All those who stayed behind never made it out of the village, of my village, the Radunovics and the Radosevics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we could go into private session and the witness could be shown Exhibit P10, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 60, after leaving your house, were you ever mobilised or did you participate in police or paramilitary operations against Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have we got an exhibit number -- we've got an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have an exhibit number, can it be admitted into evidence rather than marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what follows usually. Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One very brief matter, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel give me -- thank you, Madam Registrar. Could Defence counsel give me an indication how much time they would need for cross-examination? Mr. Emmerson or Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I should certainly be done by the end of the session today, by 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that means that you would need a little over one hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Exactly, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Five minutes if at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I should say seven just to be safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Unlikely to be any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dixon, if you could -- if it would be possible for you to finish seven minutes before the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I will certainly try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you. Then for you, Mr. Re, page 1411 gives the stipulation on line 12 in relation to the 2nd of March, which relies -- the stipulation relies on P22. It was done in the presence of your colleague Mr. Kearney. We have a break until a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon, are you ready to cross-examine Witness 60?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 60, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Dixon, who is counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Witness 60, do you know an UNMIK official from Peje by the name of Luis Perez-Segrini?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: It's correct, isn't it, that he visited you in about 2000, and he told you that you had been accused of ethnically cleansing Albanians in 1999, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. I met him in 2000 in Visoki, Decani monastery. What you are talking about took place sometime in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Fine. In 2003, did he tell you that you had been accused of ethnically cleansing Albanians, and it was alleged that you were the chief person involved in expelling Albanians from Decani municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Why did he come and tell you this information in 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: In 2003, I again visited the monastery of Decani, and before that we discussed some other things. And then during the break, he told me that somebody had something against me, there was some indictment, but he didn't show me any document nor did he take any notes about that. So quite simply, he just told me that was about that and nothing else. He didn't question me any further about the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You say he told you about some indictment. Did he tell you what the allegations were in that indictment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, he only said that there was an indictment against me, that I was the ring-leader in -- of the ethnic cleansing in the municipality of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did he tell you when he said "ethnic cleansing" what it was that you were accused of doing in Decani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, he didn't make any specific statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you ask him what these allegations were about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, I was simply sure that I couldn't have done anything like that, nor did I do anything like that, and I didn't inquire much about that. I said that I could give him the name, a few of the Albanian families that can testify to the fact that I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Well, did you ask him which Albanians were making these allegations against you and what these allegations were all about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him. I simply knew it was not true, and I didn't want to ask anything about that. After that, I often met Luis but he never mentioned it again. I even went to the Decani municipality with the -- for the group for the return of the expelled, and I met even a few Albanians. None of them ever mentioned that to me, and I never gave it a thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you not meet him again in 2005, where he told you that a group of Albanians were ready to confirm your involvement in ethnic cleansing in Dasinovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Most probably I did meet him in 2005, not once but at least five times, but he never mentioned that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Are you saying now that when you met him in 2005, on one of those occasions he did not tell you that people were ready to confirm your involvement in ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. In 2003, he mentioned that only once very briefly, and he never mentioned it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Let me try and jog your memory. It was in (redacted) that these allegations were mentioned to you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there at the time that you mentioned, and it wasn't mentioned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before my learned friend goes on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "before" --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before he continues, I wish to draw Your Honours' attention to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Line 71.7 -- page 71.7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Witness 60, referring to what I've put to you, that there was another meeting in 2005 in the place that I mentioned where the UNMIK official told you that witnesses were ready to come forward regarding an ethnic cleansing allegation, did you tell the Prosecution about that meeting when you met with them over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I used to meet with this man Luis, but he never mentioned that, even mentioned the name of a village which is next to our village. I've never been to this village and -- I mean, in the last ten years, I didn't go to that village. Secondly, except for in 2003 and Savdija Lata [phoen] was interpreter, she was from Decani, and he mentioned that only very briefly and never mentioned that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 60, I think that you did not carefully listen to the question. The question Mr. Dixon put to you is whether you told the Prosecution about the meeting just mentioned by Mr. Dixon when you met with the Prosecution over this weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I told the Prosecutor that in 2003, when I met with this man, he briefly informed me in very clear terms about that, but he never mentioned that again to me. I must say that last year I maybe met this man for another five or six times, but he also never mentioned this case to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Witness 60, let me be absolutely clear. Are you saying that you never mentioned to the Prosecution yesterday, that was Sunday, when you told them about this matter, that in 2005 you had another meeting with this UNMIK official where he told you that there were people ready to come forward to confirm your involvement in ethnic cleansing in Dasinovac, in particular? Did you never tell that to the Prosecution yesterday; yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I have to make a clarification here. Yesterday, I told the Prosecutor that I met this man sometime in 2003/2004, but most probably 2003. So I told them this yesterday, but -- can you repeat the remaining part of your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do it again. In 2005, you had a meeting with an UNMIK official where he told you that Albanians were ready to come forward to confirm your involvement in ethnic cleansing in Dasinovac. Are you saying you didn't tell the Prosecution that yesterday when you raised this matter with them? It's a yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon, a compound question and a yes and a no, sometimes it's a bit of a problem, and apart from that, the witness doesn't answer your question at this moment. Witness 60, what Mr. Dixon wants to find out is whether you had, apart from another meeting you may have had, whether you also had a meeting in which the UNMIK official told you that a group of Albanians were ready to confirm your involvement in the ethnic cleansing of Albanians in Dasinovac. Whether true or not is not the question. The question is whether you told that this was said to you by the UNMIK official and whether you said this to the Prosecution over the last weekend. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you told them that UNMIK official had told you that a group of Albanians were ready to confirm your involvement, again whether true or not; that's what you told the Prosecution yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So, Witness 60, just to have it absolutely clear then, you are now saying that you did tell the Prosecution that on two separate occasions, once in 2003 and once in 2005, you told the Prosecution that this UNMIK official told you about allegations of ethnic cleansing being made against you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dixon, this question also is not unambiguous. The 2003 and 2005 you first mentioned, and you said, You told the Prosecution; that could be understood as that in 2003 and 2005, you told the Prosecution. It could also be understood as -- you said two separate occasions; one -- you told the Prosecution. That's unclear whether the time relates to the UNMIK or to the Prosecution meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will clarify immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Witness 60, I'm talking about the meeting that you had last night, Sunday, with the Prosecution. Are you now saying that at that meeting, you told the Prosecution that there were two separate occasions, one in 2003 and one in 2005, when the UNMIK official told you about these allegations, so that you told the Prosecution last night that there were two separate occasions when these allegations were put to you by the UNMIK official. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: I understand your question, but it seems that you don't understand me. I'm saying very clearly only once in 2003 the UNMIK official conveyed this to me, and he never mentioned it again. That's what I told the Prosecutor last night; if he misunderstood me, I do apologise. So only once he told me that in 2003 and never again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon, I'm trying to clarify one thing. At that one occasion, as you tell us now, did the UNMIK official then also tell you that a group of Albanians were ready to confirm your involvement in the ethnic cleansing, again whether true or not; but was it at that one occasion that he told you about this group of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But including this information that a group of Albanians were ready to confirm your involvement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He only told me, We have some information that you were involved in this and that you were there, but he didn't mention any group or any indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Just one final question about these meetings. You said that you met this UNMIK official on a number of occasions. Did you make inquiries with him on these occasions about what was going on with these allegations that were made against you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. I never asked him anything about that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. In 1999, what was your elder brother - I'm not referring to your younger brother - your elder brother doing? Where was he working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon, is there any problem that identifying information might come up?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be safest to go into private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You said that you were in the Dasinovac area and that you could hear fighting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Dasinovac at the time. I heard shooting, but not the fighting that you're referring to, if you are referring to the shooting that was heard from Slobo Radosevic's house on the day before I left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Witness, I'm not referring to that. I'm referring to the time-period around September 1998 when you were in the Dasinovac area. Did you, when you were there, see a number of houses that were on fire that were burning down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't hear any fighting or shooting. It was very quiet at the time, and unfortunately some of the Albanian houses that I had passed by had been burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Were they still on fire at the time that you passed through the area in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you see any Serb forces, either police or army personnel, around the area when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/60
utterances.text: No. When we set off, we just inquired at the exit of Decani about the situation in our village. There was -- there were no police or any other formations there. We didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Were you aware when you were making these inquiries that there had been a major offensive by the Serbian forces in that area at the end of August and early September 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon, may I ask you to what extent the question properly reflects the evidence. The question, that's page 49.19, is -- no, it's a little bit earlier. The witness said that it was either September or October that he went back; you're now referring to early September, that's closer to August than to October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was only asking whether he, from his inquiries, knew whether there had been any forces there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but -- you said: "Were you aware when you were making these inquiries," and the inquiries according to the evidence were made just prior to going there, "that there had been a major offensive in that area at the end of August or early September?" You're linking two periods of time in a way that could be confusing and I would like you to -- it's 49.12. He said: "I went back for the first time in September or, more probably, October of that same year."

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll put the question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
